newsitem.title: USA: Congress waters down legislation on TV airwaves.
newsitem.headline: Congress waters down legislation on TV airwaves.

text.p: House and Senate lawmakers watered down legislation Wednesday that critics charged would let television broadcasters avoid key commitments they made to the government in exchange for free digital TV licenses.

The measures are attached to budget legislation that cleared both chambers of Congress and spells out cuts in Medicare, Medicaid and other federal spending programmes. Differences between the two bills must now be ironed out.

In the House, lawmakers revised language that would have allowed TV stations to keep their current analogue broadcast licenses beyond 2006 if 5 percent of their audience relies exclusively on existing over-the-air analogue signals.

In the Senate, lawmakers dropped a provision that would have encouraged -- but not required -- network-affiliated TV stations to transmit in digital format in the 30 largest cities by Nov. 1, 1999. Recent Federal Communications Commission rules require the stations to transmit such programmes by the fall of 1999.
Under the new House language, the FCC will have the power to grant extensions for the return of the analogue licenses but would not be required to do so.
The recent FCC rules require the licenses be returned by 2006, following the transition to high-definition digital TV.

Critics charged the original legislation would have left the government without a guarantee that TV stations would return the analogue specturm to the FCC for auction. And they said it would have dampened eventual bidding for the airwaves.

But broadcasters and other supporters said the original language was needed to ensure that consumers who do not buy a digital set will not be saddled with a worthless analogue set unable to receive digital signals.

A countermeasure attached to budget legislation in the Senate would allow broadcasters to keep their analogue licenses beyond 2006 -- but only in cities where less than 95 percent of the viewers have access to digital TV signals.

The provision is considered less restrictive than the original House language, because viewers can get access to digital signals through a variety of technologies -- such as cable TV, set-top converters and satellite-delivered TV.
While critics were pleased that the original language in the House bill was revised, they remained wary.

Gigi Sohn of the Media Access Project, a public-interest law firm, said the analogue provisions in the House and Senate versions were "backdoor attempts by the broadcast industry to reneg on their commitement to return the spectrum on a date certain."
She said any return of the analogue licenses would depend on the future makeup of the FCC. "I'm not happy about leaving (it) to the vagaries of future FCC," she said.
